catalog_quote: Stress is almost always word-final in the daughter languages, and it was probably also word-final in PSOG. [Daniels 2010: 168] ... Unrounded vowels in closed penults centered to /ɨ/ when followed by open ultimas; the fact that PSOG probably had word-final stress helps motivate this change. [2010: 175] ... While this innovation is not a bizarre phonetic development, the fact that these languages probably had word-final stress makes it a little peculiar. [2010: 177, on word-final nasal deletion in Manat, Mum and Sirva] ... This change may be facilitated by the prevalence of word-final stress in Manat. [Daniels 2020: 65]

new_statements.relation_note: Manat is not in the catalog and has no existing statements, so this is the first stress statement of record; it is a family-level (Sogeram) claim that covers Manat rather than a Manat-specific description.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A one-sentence family-level statement: in the Sogeram daughter languages (Manat among them; Manat data are the author's own fieldwork) stress is almost always on the last syllable of the word, and the same is reconstructed for Proto-Sogeram. No dedicated stress section, no per-language breakdown, no phonetic detail.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as 'almost always word-final'; no exceptions are listed or exemplified. The p. 177 remark treats the word-final nasal deletion of Manat, Mum and Sirva as slightly unexpected under final stress but does not revise the stress claim.
new_statements.identity_note: Manat = Paynamar (glottocode payn1244, ISO 639-3 pmr), Z'graggen's language H5. Daniels' Manat data come from his own fieldwork; no dialect is named. The 2010 paper tentatively places Manat in Central Sogeram (South Central Sogeram with Apalɨ), the 2020 book treats it under 'The Greater West Sogeram languages and Apalɨ' (section 3.2); the subgrouping shift does not affect the stress statements.

new_statements.quote: This change may be facilitated by the prevalence of word-final stress in Manat. [p. 65] ... It is worth noting that two forms which appear to match the criteria for undergoing this change did not: *kayabra 'village' > azapɨr, and PGWS *akwasa 'betelnut' > ahwas. Further research into the stress systems of the Sogeram languages might reveal a consistent pattern. [p. 60, Mand section]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Manat-specific passing remark: word-final stress is prevalent in Manat, offered as a facilitating factor for the ongoing loss of word-initial vowels (e.g. ubram ~ brʌm 'arm, hand'). The book has no stress section for any language; the p. 60 remark states that the stress systems of the Sogeram languages remain to be studied.
new_statements.exceptions: 'prevalence' rather than a categorical rule; no exceptions given. The only other stress remark (p. 60) concerns Mand, not Manat, and only says the stress systems await further research.

sources.note: Not a description; used to enumerate Daniels' Sogeram/Manat publications (2010 OL article, 2015 dissertation, 2020 De Gruyter book, PARADISEC collection DD1). Web page gives ~50 speakers in Paynamar and Simbevi, fieldwork 2010/2012/2014; no phonology.

sources.citation: Daniels, Don Roger. 2015. A Reconstruction of Proto-Sogeram: Phonology, Lexicon, and Morphosyntax. PhD dissertation, University of California, Santa Barbara. 1127 pp. (eScholarship ark:/13030/qt1kj4174g). Appendix 2 'Manat Grammar Sketch', pp. 537-657; Manat phonology = section 2.2, pp. 542-549 (pp. 567-574); ch. 2 section 2.3.2 'Manat Innovations', pp. 82-84.
sources.note: Nothing for Manat: section 2.2 covers consonant and vowel inventories, evidence for phonemic /ɨ/, phonotactics, morphophonemics (vowel elision, epenthesis, root vowel harmony) and word-initial vowel loss, with no mention of stress, accent, tone or prosody; the words 'stress'/'accent' do not occur anywhere in the 121-page sketch. The only stress remark in the entire dissertation is on p. 71 (Mand sound changes): 'Further research into the stress systems of the Sogeram languages might reveal a consistent pattern.'
